World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Choppers collide, killing 2, as fires and foreboding grip Greece
World.content:
Another three Greek firefighters died last Wednesday while tackling wildfires in Crete and on the Peloponnese, a rugged peninsula in southern Greece.

While a fire that has been burning since Friday around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth some 60 ​kilometers northwest of Athens has subsided, on Saturday the flames crossed a mountain to the south, fanned by strong winds of up to 130 kilometers per hour, and reached the settlement of Veniza closer to the capital. According to initial estimates, the fire has destroyed around 200 houses in the area.

On Sunday flames spread rapidly through western Attica, a region that encompasses Athens, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara, about 30 kilometers from the capital. Speaking on state TV Ert, the president of the firefighters’ federation, Nikos Lavranos, described it as a “huge front” and a “black blanket covering an area of around [25 acres.”

Dozens of settlements have been evacuated, and firefighters are focusing on preventing the flames from advancing toward Megara, pop. 30,000. Greece’s firefighting service said more than 2,500 people had been evacuated in western Attica by late Sunday afternoon.

“Unfortunately, we have uncontrolled fires in far too many areas. As soon as the fire brigade arrives at one spot, just as the fire is being brought under control, it flares up again in another spot,” Megara Mayor Panagiotis Margetis told Open TV.

Firefighters were also fighting another blaze in the Peloponnese on Sunday as well as on the island of Cephalonia in the Ionian Sea between Greece and Italy. More than 500 firefighters have been deployed across Greece.

World.title: Hungary faces energy crunch as drought shuts down Paks nuclear plant, PM says
World.content:
“Due to the further drop in the Danube’s water level,” Magyar wrote Saturday, “tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years."

The Soviet-built Paks facility remains the backbone of the country’s power system. The loss of output has triggered national energy-saving measures and offers of support from regional neighbors.

A prolonged outage would cripple Hungary’s electricity supply at a time when temperatures are forecast to rise above 40 degrees Celsius in Budapest next week amid an ongoing heatwave and drought across Europe.

Magyar warned the shutdown could trigger an emergency at a time of high summer demand: “An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday. Coordinated steps and self-restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences.”

The government has urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., calling on people to limit their use of air conditioning and washing machines. Authorities have also prepared an emergency plan to temporarily restrict consumption at industrial facilities on a rotating basis, while increasing output from other power plants.

The European Commission said Friday it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the Paks shutdown.

World.title: Trump cancels strikes on Iran, says deal imminent
World.content:
Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/ AFP via Getty Images

Tehran has not responded to the U.S. president’s announcement and has not confirmed an agreement to end the Middle East conflict has been reached.

U.S. President Donald Trump said late Saturday that he was canceling planned strikes on Iran pending a rapid agreement with Tehran to end the conflict in the Middle East.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump announced in a post on Truth Social.

He said the agreement would include the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” Trump added that Israel supported his commitment to pause strikes, contingent on “being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Ceuta: more migrants leave but residents still in shock. Far-right leader visits
World.content:
Here at the border between Ceuta and Morocco, the situation is much calmer than in recent days. According to Spanish authorities, the majority of the at least 60,000 people who crossed irregularly at this point on Thursday have already returned.

 

There is still a sporadic but steady stream of people heading back. Most of those returning tell us they entered Spain after receiving social media messages claiming the border was open and that no documentation was required.

Meanwhile, in the city, fear has given way to indignation. Virtually everyone I have spoken to cannot fathom how this situation could have happened and is demanding urgent explanations. It is a tense social atmosphere that is fuelling political debate.

A taxi driver told me:

"I got the feeling that people are very, very angry. I know they’re very angry right now. There are 85,000 of us here, and 60,000 are coming in. So, tell me. What do we do? What are we going to do? We can’t even buy bread. There was no bread. There was nothing. Nothing, nothing. Everything was closed."

While he was reluctant to attribute blame, some residents were more outspoken. Alluding to the initial legal difficulty of sending the migrants back immediately because they came via the sea, a middle-aged man called PM Pedro Sanchez an "accomplice", adding: "this is a disgrace— for me, a disgrace. This has never happened before in my life."

Some Ceutanos do point to a humanitarian duty in connection with the crisis. A 78-year old pensioner told me:

"If there are children there, they need to be given something to drink, they need to be given something to eat. It’s common sense, but that now all of Ceuta, all of Spain—and Spain stands with you—is with you."

However, the situation as a whole he cannot but condemn:

"This is a state of emergency and a declaration of martial law, just to go shopping at Mercadona? I have to pass a soldier every ten meters away from him ten or twenty meters away from him and feed the troops well and the police. That’s a state of siege, and it’s a of national emergency. There’s no question about it."

Santiago Abascal, the leader of Vox, visited the city today, accusing the government of being in thrall to Morocco.

Speaking to the media, Abascal placed the responsibility for what had happened on the government in Rabat and, above all, on Pedro Sánchez himself.

He argued that Morocco acted in the conviction that there would be neither response nor reprisals, because the Spanish prime minister is, in his words, "subservient to the African country".

World.title: Rupert Lowe offers alliance with Nigel Farage to unite Britain's hard right
World.content:
The leader of the UK's hard-right Restore Britain party has offered to partner with Reform UK's Nigel Farage in an effort to defeat Britain's left wing - if Farage agrees to certain conditions.

 

In a video posted to social media on Sunday, Rupert Lowe called on Farage to put "personalities" and "past disagreements" aside and work together to unite what he described as a "hopelessly divided" right.

Lowe, who was a member of parliament for Reform until 2025, when he was kicked out of the party, outlined five points that he said they would have to agree on to be able to find a "common way forward."

Firstly, Lowe said securing Britain's borders must be a priority.

"Ending mass immigration is not enough. The hour is just too late for that. It must be reversed," he said, adding: "Every illegal migrant must be deported."

Lowe's second condition centred on "demographic security" and "reversing the Islamification of Britain."

Lowe cited unspecified projections that he said showed white Britons could one day become a minority in the UK, saying: "Nothing demonstrates the demographic vandalism of mass immigration more than that."

He added that any cooperation between Restore Britain and Reform would hinge on an agreement to ban the burqa, halal and kosher slaughter, and cousin marriage, as well as "Sharia courts" and "mass dominating public Islamic prayer."

The third condition set out by Lowe was a referendum on the reintroduction of the death penalty.

"The British people must be given a full, free, and fair referendum" on the matter, he told Farage.

Britain's Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage speaks during a Reform UK rally in Wymondham, England, Tuesday July 21, 2026. PA

Fourthly, Lowe insisted they would need to commit to "restoring a self-sufficient Britain," which he said could be achieved by controlling spending, cuts to welfare, and tackling inflation.

Lowe warned "enormous cuts" would have to be made to make the plan a reality and that "difficult, unpopular decisions" would need to be taken.

His final condition was an agreement to restore trust in UK politics, as he said the country had "entirely lost faith in Westminster."

"Former Conservative ministers who failed our country and our people in so many important ways must not be part of any future cabinet," he added. "They had their chance".

Concluding his video message, Lowe said he believed that Reform and Restore Britain could find "sufficient common ground" to "destroy the looming left-wing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country."

Britain's divided right battles Burnham

Lowe's offer comes as Labour overtook Reform in two opinion polls and drew level in a third at the back end of July, as new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham made a quick start to life in Downing Street.

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, became the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade after taking over from Keir Starmer last month.

Burnham had made a dramatic return to Westminster in June after securing a large majority in the Makerfield by-election, comfortably beating out challengers from Reform UK and Lowe's Restore Britain.

The contest had been predicted to be a closer-run affair between Reform and Labour. However, Restore's stronger-than-expected performance split the right-wing vote - although not by enough to alter the result, with Burnham winning around 55% of the vote.

Since taking office, Burnham has largely focused on domestic affairs, detailing changes to the UK's education system, unveiling plans to overhaul social care, and pushing ahead with devolution pledges.

He has also announced an £8.4 billion investment into the UK's nuclear deterrent and vowed to continue support for Ukraine in its ongoing battle against Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces.

World.title: Italian Navy boards tanker from Russian shadow fleet
World.content:
Italian vessel Thaon di Revel boarded a Russian shadow fleet tanker to inspect it in international waters near Pantelleria, an island located between Sicily and Tunisia.

 

The inspection was carried out by the Italian navy on Sunday morning, 2 August, as part of the Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, the European Union mission in the Mediterranean monitoring arms and oil trafficking.

The tanker Toa Payoh, which is subject to European Union sanctions and belongs to the so-called Russian 'shadow fleet', has undergone nationality verification, which for ships is determined by the flag they are authorised to fly. The Toa Payoh is sailing under the declared flag of Cameroon.

The tanker, which left the port of Cotonou in Benin on 16 July bound for Istanbul, was intercepted west of Pantelleria. According to the ministry's account, the tanker's master initially did not provide the requested cooperation. A team of Italian military personnel then reached the vessel by helicopter from the ship Thaon di Revel and carried out the planned checks.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

"I would like to congratulate the crew of the ship Thaon di Revel and all the service personnel involved in the operation for the professionalism, preparation and resolve they have shown. This activity too is a concrete demonstration of Italy's contribution to the security of the Mediterranean and to the European Union's action," said Defence Minister Guido Crosetto.

How the operation was carried out

The Ministry of Defence reported that the operation, carried out with the support of a Greek ship and a Polish patrol aircraft, lasted around two hours and was concluded routinely and in complete safety.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

The operation, conducted in international waters under the European mandate, was carried out, the ministry note says, in full compliance with Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which allows a naval vessel, when the conditions laid down are met, to carry out the necessary checks on the nationality of a merchant ship and the flag it is authorised to fly.

At the moment, the Italian authorities are reviewing the information and documentation obtained during the inspection.

World.title: Pentagon UFO files: what role Germany plays
World.content:
Glowing objects in the sky, mysterious military reports and files kept under lock and key for decades: newly released UFO documents offer a glimpse into some of the most baffling cases of recent decades.

 

A key focus of these historical files are reports by Allied pilots from the final months of the Second World War. They described glowing flying objects moving at high speed that accompanied their aircraft over Germany. These phenomena later became known as "Foo Fighters".

In the file (source in German) (source in English), it literally states:

On the night of 22 December 1944, two lights rose from the ground near an aircraft of the 415th Night Fighter Squadron, climbed to its altitude, took up position behind its tail for about two minutes and then 'peeled away again' – according to the crew, always under 'complete control'. Ground radar confirmed that there were no enemy aircraft in the vicinity.

Such encounters were reported repeatedly. Over a period of six weeks, crews of the 415th over Germany and France spoke of red, green, orange and amber-coloured lights that flew in formation with their aircraft, carried out evasive manoeuvres and came as close as around 30 metres. The pilots called these phenomena "Foo Fighters".

The British Air Ministry examined the reports and concluded in a memorandum classified as secret in March 1945 that 'the whole matter still remains something of an enigma'.

Independently of this, pilots also reported sighting an aluminium cylinder roughly 3.6 metres long at an altitude of around 2,700 metres. When fired upon by the aircraft, the object partially lost its shape and showed a red luminous effect, but did not break apart. Intelligence classified it as probably a German 'flak bomb'.

No one was able to provide a clear explanation for the mysterious lights. The file remained classified for 80 years.

1945: A file containing reports from combat pilots Department of War

The military examined several possible explanations. One idea was that they could be previously unknown German secret weapons or experimental aircraft with novel rocket or jet propulsion systems. However, the investigations found no conclusive evidence for this.

Declassified FBI reports, "Nazi UFOs"

The released material also includes historical FBI documents from the 1940s and 1950s, in which reports appear of alleged German developments of disc-shaped flying devices. Some of these references relate to possible secret research projects in the Berlin area and in regions near the Austrian border.

However, these reports do not come from technical investigations or confirmed military files, but are based mainly on statements from informants, rumours and intelligence tips from the immediate post-war period. They therefore primarily reflect which leads the authorities chose to follow at the time.

The documents do not provide evidence that Nazi Germany actually developed operational "flying discs" with extraordinary flight performance. Historians place many of these stories in the context of speculation about German secret weapons, psychological warfare and the Allies' search for advanced German technology.

In the SHAEF and Air Ministry memoranda of 1944/45, there are repeated descriptions of, among other things, red, green, orange and amber-coloured lights that appeared to move in a controlled way, flew in formation with aircraft and in some cases came within short range of them.

Some observers report arrowhead-shaped objects. Despite this variety, certain patterns recur: many of the described craft seem to have no visible wings, rotors or conventional propulsion. They are also said to possess unusual characteristics – such as apparently motionless hovering in the air, sudden bursts of acceleration or flight manoeuvres that are difficult to explain using known technologies.

Glowing shapes, unknown flight manoeuvres

Later investigations such as the US Air Force programme Project Blue Book (1947–1969) also documented a wide range of sighting reports. Observers described, among other things, glowing geometric shapes, disc-shaped or arrow-like objects, as well as phenomena without visible wings, rotors or conventional propulsion systems. Some reports spoke of objects that appeared to hover motionless in the air, accelerate abruptly or perform flight manoeuvres that were hard to reconcile with the aviation technologies known at the time.

Alongside the historical documents, the archives contain numerous files from more recent years. Since the public revelation of the Pentagon programme AATIP (Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program) in 2017, the United States has expanded its investigations into so-called UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena).

The Department of Defense has created new structures for recording and assessing unusual observations by military personnel. The Pentagon has also released several previously classified recordings of unknown flying objects, including videos taken by Navy pilots in 2004 and 2015, whose phenomena could not initially be clearly identified.

In some documents, military personnel also report physical complaints after close encounters, such as nausea, headaches, skin irritation or neurological symptoms. What lies behind these unexplained observations remains disputed to this day. Explanations range from known technological phenomena and misperceptions to far more far-reaching hypotheses.

Recorded by an F/A-18 on 21/01/2015 off the coast of California. The video shows an elongated object flying at high speed against the wind. Navy UAP

This new transparency in the handling of Pentagon files is being closely watched in Europe as well. Security and defence experts are following the US initiatives, as unusual phenomena in airspace are increasingly viewed as a potential security and intelligence issue.

Between history and speculation

The newly released files highlight above all one thing: interest in unusual aerial phenomena goes back a long way and is closely linked to historical events such as the Second World War. Germany does feature in the documents, but the files provide no proof of extraterrestrial spacecraft or secret German "flying discs".

Rather, they document how armed forces and intelligence services have spent decades trying to explain unusual observations – and how enduring myths have grown out of them right up to the present day.

World.title: Spanish teen behind massacre threats and leader of 764 network arrested
World.content:
A joint operation involving the Guardia Civil, the autonomous police forces of the Basque Country and Catalonia (Ertzaintza and Mossos d'Esquadra) has led to the arrest in Guipúzcoa, a region near the northern border with France, of a 17-year-old Spanish national.

 

The three police forces consider him to be the main figure in Spain for the neonazi, paedophile and satanist 764 network. This organisation, which, according to the investigation, has for months been generating public alarm through threats targeting educational centres, town councils, libraries and other public and private entities.

Between January and April this year, the teenager is believed to have sent numerous messages announcing shootings and armed attacks. None were carried out, but they were enough for several institutions to activate exceptional security protocols.

In some of these messages, according to police sources, the author claimed that he would broadcast the attacks live so that other members of the organisation could watch them. Threats against a well-known leisure centre and against several individuals are also being investigated.

Searches were carried out on 16 July at two homes in Guipúzcoa linked to the suspect, once the corresponding judicial authorisations had been obtained. Officers seized electronic devices, storage media and documents which are now being analysed. The detainee has appeared before a judge and is subject to a custodial measure in a specialised centre in Donostia/San Sebastián.

What is the 764 network and how did it operate in Spain

The 764 network emerged in the United States and takes its name from the first three digits of the postcode for Stephenville, Texas, the hometown of its founder.

Over time it evolved from a marginal community on internet forums into a structure with a presence in different countries, linked to offences such as sextortion, the distribution of child sexual abuse material, incitement to self-harm, the dissemination of content showing extreme violence and animal abuse. Canada has classified it as a terrorist entity, and several countries have ongoing investigations into its activities.

In Spain, the investigation has also identified the use of techniques typical of these communities, such as swatting, doxing and identity theft, aimed at falsely pointing to people unconnected with the events in order to trigger police interventions, create dangerous situations and divert investigators' attention. At least two people, one in the Basque Country and another in Catalonia, were subjected to harassment campaigns arising from these practices.

Investigations have also revealed that the detainee took part in digital spaces where psychological manipulation was exerted on children and vulnerable young people, involving dynamics of humiliation, coercion to self-harm and submission to the will of those who recruited the victims. Images and videos obtained in this way were later shared within the community as a means of exerting control over those affected.

Prevention, the main line of defence

Investigators stress that organisations such as the 764 network actively target minors on social media, messaging apps and gaming platforms. The initial contact is usually presented as a friendship or shared interests, and only over time does it turn into manipulation, blackmail and isolating the victim from their environment.

For that reason, the authorities recommend that families and educators remain alert to signs such as requests for private photos, conversations the child hides, proposals involving self-harm or demands to take part in degrading challenges.

Early communication with the family, the school or the security forces remains, according to those responsible for the investigation, the most effective way of preventing a teenager from becoming trapped in this type of network.

World.title: Spanish government received intelligence warnings of Ceuta migrant surge according to a report
World.content:
The leader of the Popular Party, Alberto Núñez Feijoo, had already warned of the situation during his appearance yesterday in Ceuta: the Spanish Government had been aware of it since last Monday.

 

New information from several military and civilian intelligence sources suggests that the Spanish government had advance warning of the risk of a mass arrival of migrants in the North African exclave of Ceuta this week.

Intelligence alerts were issued over several days, including in the hours immediately before tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco, sources said.

Intelligence services, consulted by The Objective media, had warned that King Mohammed VI was likely to make a "gesture of magnanimity" at the border to coincide with Morocco's Throne Day celebrations. Those initial warnings were followed by reports of migrants swimming across from Fnideq, known as Castillejos in Spanish, and buses carrying people from different parts of Morocco towards the border.

Over the course of around ten days, nearly 1,000 people swam into Ceuta. Intelligence officials reportedly viewed this as a test by Moroccan authorities and passed that assessment on to the government.

In the end, between 60,000 and 75,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, marking the largest migration crisis in the autonomous city's history. According to Spain's Interior Ministry, about 53,000 people had returned to Morocco in the days that followed.

Border forces overwhelmed

The Civil Guard and National Police stationed at the Tarajal border crossing were unable to stop the influx of migrants and instead focused on assisting the injured, several sources said.

An injured migrant who crossed into Spain returns to Morocco with the assistance of a Spanish soldier from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The same sources, speaking to The Objective, criticized Madrid for not deploying the army immediately, despite military units in both Ceuta and Melilla being on standby.

"They could have been mobilized without prior meetings, simply following a political decision and an order from the operations command,” they said.

Officers deployed in the area also reported that the Moroccan gendarmerie stood "with their arms folded" while migrants attempted the crossing, both along the breakwater and on the access road to the border crossing, where other people climbed over fences and roofs.

Civil Guard sources added that the current situation differs from that seen in May 2021, when Morocco relaxed its border controls in a diplomatic response to Spain's decision to admit the Polisario Front leader, Brahim Ghali.

This time, they say, the number of people swimming into Ceuta had already been rising for weeks, partly because of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling prohibiting the immediate return of migrants who reach Spanish territory by swimming.

The government's response

The Interior Ministry insisted hours later that cooperation with Morocco was "exemplary, loyal and permanent."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the mass entry as a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity" and blamed the incident on people-smuggling networks, arguing that they had exploited the Supreme Court ruling by encouraging thousands of people to attempt the crossing.

People walk on a beach after attempting to cross from the Moroccan northern town of Fnideq to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Friday, July 31, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Sánchez also insisted that Moroccan authorities had cooperated "swiftly and consistently" from the outset, adding that Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska had reinforced border security as arrivals by sea increased.

That reinforcement ultimately resulted in about thirty additional officers and a boat that, a few days later, broke down.

Despite repeated warnings from intelligence agencies, the Ministry of the Interior did not order the deployment of reinforcements until late Thursday, when the army was called in along with additional personnel from the Civil Guard and the National Police.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest
World.content:
A suicide bomber has killed more than a dozen people including police in an attack during a demonstration of citizens against militancy. More than 18 people were injured in the attack.

A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan's northwestern Swat Valley.

Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state's inability to protect citizens.

Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence.

The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012.

Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators.

"The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station," a local police official said.

No group has claimed responsibility for the crime.

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack.

"Terrorists," said Zardari, "will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state."

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces.

The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan's military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area.

The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active.

The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries.

Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network.

World.title: Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia, killing eight
World.content:
Ukrainian drone strikes inside Russia killed eight people overnight in attacks that targeted military and civilian infrastructure. Russia said Moscow's forces downed 635 drones in the assault.

Ukrainian drones rained down on numerous military, energy and civilian infrastructure sites deep inside Russia on Sunday, killing at least eight people overnight.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 635 drones over the course of the attacks.

Two people were killed in the city of Engels on the Volga River when drones hit residential buildings. Another apartment complex in nearby Saratov City was also damaged.

Three people were reported killed and two injured in the Udmurtia region (1,300 kilometers from Ukraine), and another three killed and five injured in Belgorod according to local officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said Kyiv had targeted an oil refinery in Saratov and a military base that is home to Russian long-range bombers in Engels.

Zelenskyy said the attacks were his country's answer to Russian aggression and thanked Ukrainian forces for taking the war "back to where it came from."

Kyiv said fires had damaged both sites and that its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region.

Unverified video uploaded to social media sites purported to show fires burning at the Saratov oil facility.

Why is Ukraine targeting Wildberries warehouses?

Ukraine again targeted the online retailer Wildberries in its attacks, striking a logistics warehouse in Samara — more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's front-line positions.

Sunday's attacks on Wildberries were just the latest onslaught on the retail giant, which Kyiv says aids Russia's military.

Kyiv has attacked nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses since July 18.

No casualties were reported at the facility and local management said that a fire at the site had been brought under control.

Although the number of drones that Russia claims to have downed cannot be confirmed, the figure is indicative of the scale of Kyiv's effort to strike Russia deep inside its own territory as it defends itself against an army that launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

The Wildberries attacks are seen as an attempt to bring President Vladimir Putin's war home to Russia's citizens, applying pressure to the country's already anaemic economy in hopes of finally ending Moscow's ongoing invasion.

World.title: Ceuta: Most who breached border have left, Spain says
World.content:
08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement

Abascal called for the border with Morocco to be closed immediately Image: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO

The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy.

Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.

Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties.

The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush.

The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion."

He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards."

Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped.

Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent.

Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police.

Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani.

Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area.

World.title: Greece: Fire brigade helicopters collide as wildfires spread
World.content:
The crew of one of the helicopters is reported to be safe but the search for the second is ongoing. Prime Minister Mitsotakis has warned of "extremely difficult" days ahead, while one expert has referred to a "megafire."

Two fire brigade helicopters collided mid-air in Greece on Sunday, as firefighters continued to battle fierce wildfires around the Gulf of Corinth.

The fire service said the two aircraft collided in the Psatha area, just to the west of the capital, Athens, adding that search and rescue teams were "immediately mobilized to locate and assist the crews."

Television footage showed one of the helicopters explode and plunge to the ground in flames after an apparent rotor collision.

Greek public broadcaster ERT reported that the crew of one of the helicopters had been found and were safe. The fate of the crew of the second helicopter initially remained unclear.

Greece wildfires: 'Extremely difficult' days ahead, says PM

The accident came as Greek firefighters continued to battle wildfires on multiple fronts. Three firefighters died in recent days in the line of duty, two in Crete and one in the Peloponnese.

Greek firefighters struggle to save coastal resort To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fires are being exacerbated and spread by winds of up to 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis warning of "extremely difficult" days ahead.

"When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely," he wrote on social media.

"There are moments when nature and the intensity of weather phenomena surpass any human planning and any operational capability."

Volunteers battle a wildfire burning near Porto Germeno Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Just to the north of Psatha in the neighboring town of Porto Germeno, nearly 500 firefighters were attempting to keep a blaze from approaching the western outskirts of Athens after it scaled a mountain overnight.

Footage released by Greek police showed officers going door to door on motorcycles in the nearby hilltop village of Agios Nektarios, sounding sirens and shouting "Is anyone there?" as they urged residents to evacuate.

On Friday, firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea – often the last escape route for isolated coastal communities – followed by another 12 on Saturday.

"We could not believe what we were seeing," Nikos Georgopoulos from the laboratory of forest management at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, told state TV channel ERT. "The fire spread extremely rapidly."

Greece: man arrested on suspicion of arson

Further west and on the opposite side of the Gulf of Corinth, some 100 firefighters were fighting another blaze in Aigialia in the northern Peloponnese region.

Three firefighters have lost their lives while on duty Image: Michael Varaklas/AP Photo

Meanwhile, a 44-year-old man was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of deliberately starting a new fire which broke out late Saturday on the popular Ionian Sea island of Cephalonia.

The National Observatory's climate tracker meteo.gr said early estimates indicated that over 6,500 hectares (16,000 acres) had been burned in separate fires around the Gulf of Corinth.

Meteorologist Theodore Giannaros said that the fires around Porto Germeno are "likely, if not almost certain … [to] be classified as a megafire."
