World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Cut-price cars, pay rises and trips by foster care charity execs face scrutiny
World.content:
A New South Wales charity responsible for finding foster homes for children spent more than $40,000 of taxpayer money to send its chief executive on a "sabbatical" to the US and Europe.

That same year, it awarded the individual a $120,000 pay rise, allegedly without "discussion or formal approval", boosting their salary by two-thirds.

Taxpayer money was also allegedly misused on Airbnb stays, rugby league sponsorships, parties, alcohol and more.

The ABC is not naming the organisation accused in a confidential forensic audit of misusing taxpayer funds for legal reasons.

The charity had received tens of millions of dollars under state government Permanent Support Program (PSP) contracts, to help more than 100 children under 18 years old find foster homes, mostly in Greater Sydney.

It is not the only organisation holding PSP contracts that is suspected of fraudulently using taxpayer funds.

The ABC understands five others are being targeted by the Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ).

Three of the organisations have to meet new conditions to keep their PSP contracts.

Three others are not having their contracts renewed and will no longer be allowed to find foster homes for children and teenagers.

The ABC is not naming the five other providers for legal reasons.

Overseas trips, cars and events a concern

The Department of Communities and Justice is targeting a number of organisations that find foster homes for children and young people. (Pixabay, truthseeker08)

A "high volume of complaints" against the chief executive, "financial impropriety, and a perceived lack of board oversight", were some of the reasons why the DCJ ordered a forensic audit into one foster care organisation in Greater Sydney.

The confidential forensic audit covered operations from October 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025, when more than 99 per cent of the charity's funding came from taxpayers, exceeding $34 million.

Independent firm BDO Services said $1.6 million had not been recorded because the organisation under-reported the interest it made from funds, overcharged or double charged services, and had not documented some of the assets it sold.

In addition to uncovering unaccounted-for money, the auditors flagged several expenses as "potentially non-compliant", because they had no clear link to the work it was contracted to carry out.

Travel was a "key concern" with more than $98,000 flagged.

This included almost $41,500 spent on a sabbatical to the US and Europe for its chief executive, and about $8,600 for a trip to New Zealand for the chief executive, the deputy chief executive, and chair of the board.

A smaller share of money is finding its way to the children and young people in need. (Pexels)

Another concern was a pay increase secured by the chief executive, as their salary of $181,761 jumped to $300,574 in the financial year ending in 2024, an increase of 65 per cent.

"Based on the Board minutes reviewed, we did not identify discussion or formal approval relating to the performance or remuneration of the CEO," the audit read.

" On the material available, it is unclear when, by whom, or through which governance process the annual pay increases were approved. "

Other transactions flagged by the forensic audit included:

Five cars sold to staff, family and friends at up to 55.3 per cent below the market rate

$226,971.72 for advertising and promotion, including the sponsorship of five football teams and events, mostly in regions the charity did not service

$22,876.16 on catering, make-up services, office amenities and entertainment

$14,978.10 on coaching lessons for the CEO and the Board

$6,709.09 on a security system and door camera installed at the CEO's residential address

$10,123.84 on food and alcohol at restaurants and hotels, both in Australia and overseas

'Genuinely shocked'

Ms Washington says the status quo is unacceptable. (ABC News: Emily Jane Smith )

The cost of finding foster homes for children and young people soared by 239 per cent during a six-year period to 2024, according to state government figures, increasing from $322 million to $1.1 billion.

Executive and corporate manager fees tripled, from $38 million to $117 million.

Meanwhile, a smaller share of money found its way to the children and young people in need, dropping from 43 per cent to 30 per cent.

"I was genuinely shocked to find that the system that was created was allowing funding to flow away from vulnerable children and towards the financial interests of individuals and providers," NSW Government Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington said.

"One of the very first reports to land on my desk was about young children not even having the winter school uniform they needed to stay warm at school, despite the provider receiving millions of dollars in funding to provide services to those kids."

Years of reform ahead

The NSW government said one of the issues with the current foster care system was the "weak accountability for delivery of services".

NSW unveils sweeping foster care reforms for vulnerable children While some child protection services will continue to be outsourced, the NSW government will play a larger role in the sector, including through the recruitment of foster carers.

It is changing the out-of-home-care strategy in stages until 2030.

"A large part of our reforms is ensuring that we are introducing stronger measures around accountability and transparency," Ms Washington said.

"Contracts will require information to be provided to us that wasn't required before, in terms of where and how they are spending their money."

Part of the reform process is phasing out the PSP contracts held by providers.

Shadow Families and Communities Minister Natasha Maclaren-Jones said the government should focus more on early prevention programs to lower the number of kids needing foster care.

"At the end of the day, it's about ensuring that the standards we have in place are workable and that children are being protected," she said.

"And of course, taxpayers' funds are being used appropriately."

World.title: Ben Carroll to fill one of three vacancies in Victorian cabinet, ABC understands
World.content:
The ABC understands Victorian Premier Ben Carroll will fill just one of the three vacancies in cabinet when caucus meets on Monday morning.

The meeting was planned to discuss the vacancies left following former premier Jacinta Allan's resignation last week and to fill the frontbench position.

Last Tuesday, Ms Allan announced she would stand down ahead of an expected spill motion she was tipped to lose.

It was somewhat unexpected having, just 24 hours earlier, written to Labor's state secretary to confirm she would contest any leadership ballot.

A caucus meeting to elect a new leader descended into chaos after Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny put her hand up for the leadership, which would have triggered a wider vote involving rank-and-file party members.

The process, which could have taken several weeks, was avoided when Ben Carroll was unanimously elected as premier.

Transport Infrastructure Minister Gabrielle Williams was elected his deputy.

Jacinta Allan leaving a caucus meeting following her resignation. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mordialloc MP to be promoted

Just days after Ms Allan stood aside, ministers Harriet Shing and Lily D'Ambrosio also announced their resignations from cabinet.

Health minister Ms Shing was a close ally of Ms Allen and Ms D'Amborio was Australia's longest-serving energy and climate minister.

Their departure left three positions in cabinet for the new premier to fill.

Despite that, MPs have told the ABC that Mr Carroll had determined he would only fill just one of the positions.

Tim Richardson is expected to progress to cabinet in Ms Allan's absence. (ABC News)

He had previously promised Ms Allan's position to Tim Richardson, who is expected to be elevated today.

The Mordialloc MP was a government advisor before entering parliament more than a decade ago. He was recently promoted to cabinet secretary.

All three vacancies were in the Socialist Left, which has been left in tatters after last week's events.

The Socialist Left has for years enjoyed dominance in Labor's factions — blocs within the Labor Party of MPs and powerbrokers aligned on policy and other interests. It was also home to former premier Daniel Andrews.

World.title: Suspended SA principal cleared of 'misconduct'
World.content:
A South Australian school principal has been cleared of "misconduct" by the Education Department after being abruptly stood down from her job.

In November, the department suspended Tamarin Condon from her position as principal of Wallaroo Mines Primary School in Kadina.

Before she was stood down, Ms Condon was the subject of a petition circulated online which called on the department to "urgently review" her leadership and expressed concerns about alleged "unprofessional behaviour".

At the time, then-education minister Blair Boyer confirmed reports she had invited her husband, Simon Condon, to assist at a school camp.

Mr Condon had worked as a student support officer but was not employed by the school.

In a brief statement, a Department spokesperson said:

"The Department for Education has concluded its investigation. No misconduct was identified." "A new Principal has been appointed to Wallaroo Mines Primary School. "For privacy reasons, we do not intend to comment further about this matter."

The department said it could not comment on what lines of inquiry were pursued during their investigation, citing privacy.

The ABC reported in December that parents said Department for Education officials had quizzed students who attended the camp about Ms Condon's behaviour.

At the time, two parents said they had spoken to SA Police, and a police spokesperson confirmed they were aware of the matter.

"There is no police investigation at this time. Enquiries should be directed to the Department for Education," the spokesperson had said.

In a statement, Ms Condon's lawyer, Luke Officer, said his client welcomed the findings.

"Allegations are only that until they are otherwise proven," Mr Officer said.

"Investigations into allegations must proceed without unhelpful public commentary that can damage reputations unnecessarily and without justification.

"As the Department has concluded there was no misconduct after a thorough investigation, this matter is a timely reminder of those fundamental principles.

"My client welcomes its closure and to moving on."

World.title: 'Sohos, apartments and lofts' proposed for leafy Macedon Ranges hamlet
World.content:
The rural hamlet of Clarkefield sits at the edge of the leafy Macedon Ranges and is home to about 300 people, a small train station, a closed pub, and a fire shed.

But a $700 million housing development plans to change all that.

The proposal includes 2,500 homes for more than 6,000 new residents, but there is a catch.

Some of the proposed lots are as small as 84 square metres, a size more commonly found in inner-city Melbourne, while many others are less than 300sqm.

Developer APD Projects said the "apartments, lofts, sohos, townhouses and terraces" would transform Clarkefield's paddocks and lifestyle blocks into a medium to high-density "village".

Angela Tiede says housing estate plans shown to some residents in 2021 do not mirror those sent to the planning minister for fast-tracked approval. (Supplied: Fred Kroh / Creekstories.net)

Angela Tiede was impressed with APD Project's vision when it was introduced to residents in 2020.

She liked the "new, smaller and sustainable" village that reflected the township's history and loved the idea of a community farm and renewable energy system.

But, according to Ms Tiede, those plans have been replaced by ones "that are so far from that, it's laughable".

Clarkefield sits at the edge of the Macedon Ranges. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)

Residents said APD Projects has misled them and the plans submitted to the Victorian planning minister for approval do not reflect what was shown to residents.

"I was thinking it was the original proposal, and it was only when someone said to me, 'Actually no, I think you should look at this again', it is absolutely not what was talked about," Ms Tiede said.

"So I think the developers have really tried to play a shifty here.

"To cram people into multi-storey buildings, they're talking three- and four-storey buildings, and still saying they're maintaining the atmosphere of the village, well that's just preposterous, really."

Before: The main road in to Clarkefield station is bordered by open fields. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson) . . After: Plans for the proposed housing development at Clarkefield show land lots between 84 and 400 square metres. (Supplied: APD Projects) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The main road in to Clarkefield station is bordered by open fields. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson) / Plans for the proposed housing development at Clarkefield show land lots between 84 and 400 square metres. (Supplied: APD Projects)

A number of other residents the ABC has spoken to were worried about the conditions of local roads, traffic congestion, not enough carriages on the nearby train to support thousands more residents and said the blocks were far too small.

They also disliked the "cookie-cutter" modern style of homes slated for the area and said water tables, estuaries and flood plains needed to be properly assessed.

Concept plans for the proposed housing estate at Clarkefield show a mix of high-density homes and retail next to the existing train station. (Supplied: APD Projects)

Modern look for rural character

The vision for Clarkefield began when landholder Rupert Clarke approached APD Projects and its partners about creating a compact and connected walkable village.

His great-great-grandfather Sir William Clarke was a pastoralist from Tasmania and surveyed 12,500 hectares of land as the gold rush took hold in Victoria.

Design guidelines released by APD Projects show modern townhouses with rendered facades and an urban centre for shops.

But the $700 million development is already causing tension after residents and civic leaders failed to fight off a development in nearby Riddells Creek.

The Macedon Ranges Shire Council has seen its role as the responsible planning authority handed to the minister for planning under the state's controversial Development Facilitation Program (DFP).

The program bypasses local planning authorities, and opportunities for residents and councils to appeal, and leaves the final decision at the minister's discretion.

Sonya Kilkenny will announce her decision on the Clarkefield development in September. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

In a new submission to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny in July, councillors called for its planning powers to be returned and for an independent planning panel and advisory committee to assess the application because of its numerous "deficiencies".

Kate Kendall, who resigned from her role as Macedon Ranges mayor in July to run as the Liberal candidate for the seat of Macedon at the upcoming November state election, said the Clarkefield estate was one of the biggest planning proposals to come before the council.

Ms Kendall said she was worried the development went against planning guidelines and protections placed over the Macedon Ranges in 2020.

"People really need to know what community they're moving into and what supports are there," she said.

"Communities, their voice, should be the number one thing and not cut out from large decision-making.

"These decisions, which are triggering a lot of community backlash, are being driven by a sole decision-maker."

'You call 84 square metres a lot?'

Macedon Ranges Residents Association secretary Christine Pruneau has spent decades fighting state and local governments about planning decisions and amendments in the Macedon Ranges.

She said giving a green light to the Clarkefield estate would be a reversal of the Labor Party's promise in 2020 to protect towns in the Macedon Ranges from inappropriate development.

Christine Pruneau says the decision-making process bypasses checks and balances for new housing development. (Supplied: Christine Pruneau)

" You call 84 square metres a lot?" she said. "You'd have to say that they're hardly big enough for a dunny. "

She said the approval of the nearby Amess Road development at Riddells Creek, and the impending decision for Clarkefield, had created a worrying precedent for areas that had distinctive landscapes.

"The minister for planning appears to be easily led with an amenable department because they've gone gung-ho for this proposal, using the developer's documentation to run what comes across as a secret amendment," she said.

"Anybody can just take over and become dictators. There's no planning sense in what's being done.

"There's no strategic work. It's all been done by the developer, and you would have to be looking for bias."

Ms Pruneau wants the government to bring back transparent and public planning, adhere to the Statement of Planning Policy that protects development in the Macedon Ranges, and appoint an independent assessment for the Clarkefield development.

The Clarkefield Hotel is one of the historic buildings near the planned development. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)

The council stated in 2020 it did not want to compromise future development of Clarkefield, despite it not being a priority area, but said any development would need to come with suitable infrastructure and services.

In July, council said the Clarkefield estate posed future financial risk to develop and maintain the infrastructure and services 6,000 residents would need.

It said there were potential social effects of placing that many people in an isolated location without education, health, employment, community services and affordable housing.

However, APD Projects's plans show a super-lot of 140 affordable homes is included in the first stage of the development, which will be delivered in partnership with Assemble, an affordable housing provider for low- and middle-income people.

Before: Clarkefield sits at the edge of the Macedon Ranges. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson) . . After: Plans for Clarkefield show modern, two-storey houses on blocks as small as 84 square metres. (Supplied: APD Projects) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Clarkefield sits at the edge of the Macedon Ranges. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson) / Plans for Clarkefield show modern, two-storey houses on blocks as small as 84 square metres. (Supplied: APD Projects)

Changing scenery

APD Projects was started in 2013 by its founder and director, Brad Paddon.

He and his team have spent the past five years working on the Clarkefield estate and chose to get planning approval through the DFP.

Brad Paddon says APD Projects wants to establish a sustainable township that is carbon neutral. (Supplied: APD Projects)

He rejected the claim residents had been misled and said the plans still showed the "new, smaller and sustainable way of doing things" originally pitched to residents.

He said some things had changed since the minister for planning referred the development to the DFP in October 2024, such as traffic and vegetation, but disagreed that the lot sizes and style of housing did not belong in the Macedon Ranges.

"We've taken a lot of cues from townships in and around the Macedon Ranges, and we have design guidelines that help us borrow Macedon Ranges character and implement that in new homes," he said.

" Undoubtedly, we will be bringing new housing typologies that are not common in the Macedon Ranges. "

The historic Stables is one of the few buildings currently near Clarkefield station. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)

Mr Paddon would not comment on whether increasing the lot sizes and lowering the density of housing would make the project less viable for APD Projects and "its Melbourne families" backing the development.

He said he supported the DFP planning pathway and said questions of transparency and community input were for the Victorian government to answer.

"We've just utilised a planning pathway that has been made available to us," Mr Paddon said.

He said the Clarkefield estate would still use solar panels, low-energy products and establish a 5-megawatt solar farm to the north of the township, and a community farm.

In a statement, Ms Kilkenny said any proposal would be considered on its merits.

"As this project is currently under assessment, it would be inappropriate to comment further," the statement read.

The statement also said the Macedon Ranges Statement of Planning Policy did not preclude any particular forms of housing within the Macedon Ranges Distinctive Area and Landscape.

World.title: Minister instructs Qld Health to review 'discriminatory' fertility guidance
World.content:
Queensland's health minister has instructed the state's health department to review its fertility clinic guidance after several women were told they could not proceed with their treatments.

It follows ABC reporting of a lesbian couple who were informed they were no longer the same family under Queensland Health guidelines and told they may not be able to conceive using the same sperm donor.

In Queensland, donated sperm or eggs cannot be used to create more than 10 Australian families, which the state's legislation defines as a parent, their children and their spouse, if any.

But in February, Queensland Health released general guidance advising fertility providers to count lesbian couples who both conceive using the same donor as two separate families.

Surrogacy and fertility lawyer Stephen Page said Queensland Health's interpretation of the donor-related family limit was "clearly discrimination against lesbian couples".

Fertility lawyer Stephen Page said Queensland Health's family limit guidance contradicts several other pieces of state and federal legislation. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"The legislation is quite clear that family is you, your partner and your children," he said.

"We've long recognised lesbian couples under the Status of Children Act in Queensland and under the Family Law Act, and of course under the Marriage Act."

" So then to say, 'Well, we recognise everyone else, but we don't recognise you' really does not pass the pub test. "

While the health department is due to complete its review in the coming weeks, Queensland women and fertility clinics are still subject to the "discriminatory" guidance.

'Heartbreaking' impact on patients

Deborah Poerio, 36, has been trying to get pregnant through IVF for six years. After creating four embryos in April, she thought she may finally get the chance.

However, in a "heartbreaking" call on July 23 from her fertility provider, Monash IVF, she was told she could not go ahead with an embryo transfer because there were no more family spots available with her sperm donor.

Ms Poerio has been trying to get pregnant through IVF for six years. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

In a follow-up email, the clinic told Ms Poerio there were 10 families allocated to her donor, one or more of which were same-sex couples who, under the updated guidance, now used more family spots.

Qld Health guidance changes family definition for lesbians The Queensland Health advice, issued in February, has had a "devastating" impact on some same-sex couples trying to have more children.

"Until Monash IVF received further guidance from Queensland Health about the interpretation of the family limit, these couples had been considered as one family allocation," the clinic wrote in an email.

"As a result of this clarified advice, we are required to apply individual allocations under the family limit.

"This is why you were previously able to create embryos using this donor, but following the clarified advice, the donor is now considered to be over the family limit under the Queensland ART Act."

Ms Poerio was crushed by the news.

"The embryos are mine," she said.

"They are not property of Queensland Health.

"I created them with pain and with hope and they step in and say, 'You actually can't [transfer] because we misinterpreted the law'.

"No thank you, let me transfer my embryo."

Monash IVF applied to Queensland Health to allow Ms Poerio to use her embryos, and eight days later, the department granted her an approval.

But Ms Poerio said she felt it was "ridiculous" she needed to ask for an exemption in the first place.

"It has been a week filled with headaches, tears, worries, heartbreak and no-one is going to give me this week back," she said.

" No-one is going to give me that happiness that has been taken away from a week of my life. "

Guidance review as 'matter of priority'

In a statement, Health Minister Tim Nicholls said he had received and considered feedback about Queensland's family limit guidelines.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls has asked the health department to review its fertility guidance "as a matter of priority". (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"I share many of the concerns that have been raised in relation to the Department of Health's interpretation of the law and guidance to service providers," he said.

"I have asked the department to seek further advice as a matter of priority, and that guidance materials be reviewed following the provision of this advice."

The ABC understands this review process is expected to be complete within a matter of weeks.

Advocate calls for immediate clarification

Michelle Galea, founder of Assisted Reproductive Treatment Families Australia and Australian Solo Mothers by Choice, said Queensland Health was "making the donor pool smaller for no good reason" by requiring lesbian couples to use two family allocations.

Michelle Galea is the founder of Assisted Reproductive Treatment Families Australia and Australian Solo Mothers by Choice. (Supplied)

"I want a clarification and I need it today," Ms Galea said.

"We can't wait another month, we can't wait another two weeks.

"We have got women who are in the midst of their procedures and their mental health is just debilitating."

In a statement, a spokesperson for Monash IVF said the company understood "how distressing the recent regulatory changes to donor limits in Queensland have been for patients across the IVF sector".

"Monash IVF supports family limits to protect donor-conceived people and would support a national approach to these regulations," the spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for Monash IVF said the company would support Queensland Health in a review of its regulations. (AAP image: James Ross)

"However, the new regulations in Queensland, which revise the definition of a family, are having unintended consequences for some patients, affecting their ability to access treatment using their existing donor embryos.

"Monash IVF is in discussions with Queensland Health and would support Queensland Health in a review of the regulations to ensure they achieve the intended purpose while also supporting continuity of care for patients, especially those who created embryos before the new regulations came into effect."

Queensland Health was contacted for comment.

World.title: Sunny reprieve ahead for south-east Queensland as windy Ekka week looms
World.content:
Queensland's east coast can expect a "brief reprieve" from showery conditions later this week before a potentially windy Ekka week.

Much of the state's east coast was peppered with showers over the weekend, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

The most frequent falls were around the north tropical coast, particularly around the Cassowary Coast, where more than 70 millimetres of rain was recorded in the 24 hours to 9am Sunday.

The south-east also experienced showers over the weekend, with the Sunshine Coast seeing the highest totals of 10 to 20 millimetres.

Sunny conditions are forecast for later this week in the south-east. (ABC Gold Coast: Charmayne Allison)

In comparison, inland parts were "relatively settled", according to senior forecaster Felim Hanniffy.

This included dry conditions and some cool mornings with temperatures as low as minus 1.5 degrees Celsius on Saturday around parts of the Granite Belt.

Showers expected to ease

Mr Hanniffy said showers were expected to ease in the coming days along central and southern coasts due to a "surge of south-westerly airflow".

Dry and mostly sunny conditions were forecast for these areas by the middle of the week, but the forecaster warned the reprieve would be brief.

"Later in the week, we'll see some of those coastal showers return to part of the east coast again for Friday and into the weekend," he said.

Showers will become more isolated along the north tropical coast later in the week. (ABC Far North: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

He said the area would include much of the south-east including the Gold Coast, Brisbane and the Sunshine Coast, all the way up to the Wide Bay Burnett and possibly the Capricornia.

"But we're talking at this stage, only light falls," he said.

Mr Hanniffy said showers would also be on a "slow-easing trend" along the north tropical coast in the days ahead.

"But they're not going to completely clear and by the middle of the week will be a bit more isolated," he said.

The north tropical coast saw more than 70 millimetres of rain over the weekend. (ABC Far North: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

The forecaster said overnight minimum temperatures were expected to remain "a bit on the cool side" throughout the state's interior this week.

Patchy frost was possible for the southern interior over the coming days, with a chance of more "extensive areas of frost" across the region by the middle of the week.

Potentially windy Ekka week

Mr Hanniffy said "quite fresh" south-easterlies were currently in play along the east coast, particularly the north-east tropical coast.

A strong wind warning was in place today for the Torres Strait, Peninsula Coast and Cooktown Coast.

South-east Queensland has been warned to brace for windy conditions next week. (ABC Gold Coast: Charmayne Allison)

"We'll see those winds gradually easing back during Tuesday and Wednesday," Mr Hanniffy said.

He warned "more significant weather systems" could move across southern parts of the state next week.

"This could bring some quite windy conditions during in the lead up to the Ekka," he said.

"So while this week looks pretty benign, certainly the week after we could see some gusty windy changes moving through at times."

World.title: Gliders were thought to eat swift parrots. Cameras showed something different
World.content:
A new study has called into question the extent to which introduced sugar gliders prey on critically endangered swift parrots in Tasmania, pointing instead to habitat loss as the overarching risk to the species.

The Commonwealth-funded study, by landscape ecologist Matt Webb and veterinary ecologist Leanne Wicker, included acoustic monitoring, motion cameras and glider trapping over two breeding seasons on mainland Tasmania.

They could not find examples of sugar gliders killing swift parrots.

The study monitored 20 nests across two breeding seasons in various regions of Tasmania. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

"No confirmed predation of swift parrots by sugar gliders was recorded during this study, despite documented visitation to and entry into nest hollows," the study reads.

"Gliders were detected at, and inside, nests that successfully fledged young, confirming that presence or visitation alone is not a reliable indicator of impact."

A sugar glider is captured investigating a tree hollow that contains a swift parrot nest. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

The study found both successful and failed nests in the same areas, including where sugar gliders were present.

But rather than sugar glider predation, there was evidence of birds, including native currawongs and introduced European starlings, preying on swift parrots in nests, although "no species determined nest success or failure".

Loading...

European starlings attacked and killed swift parrots. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

A black currawong is among the native birds that were seen to take swift parrot chicks. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

The study authors put this down to competition-related aggression, as well as predation, exacerbated by "ongoing habitat loss and fragmentation".

"Breeding success is shaped by multiple interacting ecological processes, and conservation planning should reflect this," it reads.

A boobook owl next to a tree hollow containing a swift parrot nest. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

Researchers take 'contemporary' approach

For more than a decade, sugar gliders have been considered a main threat to the swift parrot on mainland Tasmania, reducing their survival rate to as low as 17 per cent, based on earlier studies.

But Dr Webb said this did not align with his experiences in the field.

Ecologists Matt Webb and Leanne Wicker say the "narrative" around sugar gliders did not match what they saw in the field. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

They obtained a grant from the Commonwealth's Saving Native Species program to build on the evidence around the interactions between sugar gliders and swift parrots.

"What we wanted to do is bring a contemporary approach, a focus on the monitoring nests on mainland Tasmania using a whole range of approaches," Dr Wicker said.

"Understanding glider diet using forensic necropsies, to understand why swift parrots died when we found nest failure.

"We were able to interpret that from the context of two decades of monitoring swift parrots in the wild."

Acoustic monitoring identified where swift parrots were nesting, and cameras were set up at 20 nests for periods of more than two months each.

Necropsies were carried out on swift parrots that had died as well as on trapped gliders, to determine whether they were eating the parrots.

Necropsies were carried out on sugar gliders captured near swift parrot nests. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

Dr Wicker said the dead parrots did not display signs of being killed by sugar gliders, while the glider diet did not contain any evidence of parrots.

"The sugar glider diet looked exactly like what we see on mainland Australia; they are a plant-eating species, they mainly eat eucalypts and acacias with some insects," she said.

Government wanted to paint gliders as 'the main threat'

Based on previous studies, the Tasmanian government has sought to emphasise sugar gliders as the major risk to swift parrots, as opposed to habitat loss from native forest logging.

What happened when a rare bird found a place to nest near a logging coupe It was late 2021 when one of Australia's rarest birds started to arrive in the native forests of Lonnavale. Ecologists had expected it but for a reacting forestry sector, it was "not sustainable".

This included suggested edits to the swift parrot recovery plan, in which the state government wanted predation by sugar gliders listed as "the main threat to the survival of swift parrot".

The government threatened to withdraw its endorsement of the document unless a "narrative focus" on its forestry management system was addressed.

While earlier studies pointed to sugar gliders as killing female parrots and eggs, they also stated that this was less of a risk in wider swathes of mature forest.

Swift parrots breed in Tasmania over spring and summer before migrating annually to the Australian mainland. (Supplied: Billy Rowe)

Dr Webb said the narrative around swift parrot survival had since changed to make sugar gliders a "scapegoat".

"Sugar gliders are just one of the threats, but all of them sit underneath like an umbrella of habitat loss," he said.

" The conversation around swift parrot predation and swift parrot conservation has become really binary, it's either habitat loss or predation by sugar gliders, but that's not real. "

Dr Webb said this made it difficult to obtain research funding for swift parrots, compared with funds for sugar glider research.

Swift parrot and clearfelling It was late 2021 when one of Australia's rarest birds started to arrive in the native forests of Lonnavale. Ecologists had expected it but for a reacting forestry sector, it was "not sustainable".

Focus on habitat protection

Mark Holdsworth first identified the potential risk posed by sugar gliders during research into the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot in Tasmania over two decades ago.

His work prompted further studies.

Mark Holdsworth OAM is the chair of BirdLife Tasmania. (Supplied)

Dr Holdsworth said the new study showed the sugar glider did not appear to be as important a predator as previously thought, and that there were other pressures.

But he said addressing all predators would be impossible.

"A lot of those predators we can't do anything about; they're there in our landscape, they've been well established," Dr Holdsworth said.

" What we can do is protect the remaining habitat. "

Sugar gliders are believed to have been introduced to Tasmania in the late 19th century.

Finding swift parrot nests is difficult, researchers say, and installing equipment at their hollows takes considerable effort. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

In a review earlier this year for the journal Australian Forestry, Simon Grove assessed previous studies to compare the "forest habitat narrative" with the "predation narrative", arguing there was more evidence for the latter.

He suggested sugar gliders could be eradicated through gene drives, while also acknowledging forest harvesting "may not make things any easier for the parrots".

The latest study has come out after his review.

Scrutiny on logging system

The swift parrot's status was uplifted from endangered to critically endangered in 2016 due to concerns about the impact of sugar gliders.

Sugar gliders have been considered a major threat to swift parrots, which has been emphasised by the Tasmanian government. (Supplied: Landscape Recovery Foundation)

In its recovery plan, sugar gliders are mentioned first in the threats section, followed by loss or degradation of habitat through logging, land clearing and wildfire.

Swift parrot numbers could be as low as 500.

Tasmania's forest logging system includes increased habitat protection in swift parrot important breeding areas, but studies have shown the overall extent of logging is greater in these areas.

A logged area in the Lonnavale forests, near where swift parrots had been seen nesting. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Foraging habitat is protected and potential nest trees are mapped prior to logging.

Trees above a certain size are intended to be excluded from logging but can still be cut down for safety reasons.

The area is then burnt and re-sown after logging, but studies have shown a progressive degradation of habitat over time.

Public forestry company Sustainable Timber Tasmania has previously stated that the swift parrot faces "multiple interacting threats", while describing sugar gliders as "the principal driver" of population decline.

World.title: Suicide bomber strikes crowd at anti-militant rally in Pakistan
World.content:
A suicide bomber has targeted protesters at an anti-militant rally in north-western Pakistan, killing at least 14 people, mostly civilians and police officers, and wounding more than two dozen others, according to officials.

The attack happened in Kabal, a town in Swat Valley in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where demonstrators had gathered near a police station, chanting anti-militant slogans and demanding peace, district police chief Omar Khan said.

According to witnesses, shortly before the attack, speakers at the rally said ensuring security and eliminating militancy were the state's responsibility.

They also accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, saying residents wanted to live without fear after years of violence that devastated the region.

The Swat Valley is a former stronghold of Islamic militants. (AP: Sherin Zada)

Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial emergency service, said the attacker struck dozens of people who were chanting anti-militant slogans and demanding peace.

Police official Omar Khan said at least nine civilians and five officers were among the dead.

Pakistan and the Taliban edge closer to 'open war' Pakistan's declaration of an "open war" with the Afghan Taliban sounds dangerous, but analysts say neither side has the capacity to win.

Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the bombing, expressing deep sorrow over the loss of life.

In separate statements, they offered condolences to the families of those killed, prayed for the recovery of the wounded and directed authorities to ensure the wounded receive the best possible medical treatment.

Mr Zardari and Mr Sharif also said Pakistan's fight against terrorism would continue until it was eradicated.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also condemned the attack. In a statement, he extended condolences to the families of those killed and prayers for the speedy recovery of the wounded.

Suspicion lands on resurging Pakistani Taliban

The Swat Valley was once a stronghold of Islamic militants who imposed a strict interpretation of Sharia, or Islamic law, before the Pakistani military launched a major operation in 2007 that drove them out and restored government control.

However, militants have resurfaced in Pakistan's Swat Valley in recent months, fuelling fears that the Pakistani Taliban is seeking to regain a foothold in the region. In response, residents have repeatedly staged anti-Taliban rallies to protest the militants' presence across the valley.

Pakistan declares 'open war' against Afghanistan Pakistan was responding to "unprovoked fire" by Afghan forces at multiple locations along the border, the Information Ministry in Islamabad says.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the bombing, but suspicion is likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP.

The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers. Many of its leaders and fighters have found sanctuary in Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power there in 2021.

Pakistan has long accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring TTP militants, an allegation Kabul denies.

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks in recent years, particularly targeting police and security forces.

On Friday, Pakistan's military spokesman Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan had recorded 3,145 "terrorism incidents" since January. He said Pakistan had killed 2,084 militants since January, while 819 Pakistanis, including soldiers, police officers and civilians, had been killed.

Chaudhry also said Afghanistan-based militants had carried out 28 suicide attacks in Pakistan since January and alleged that most were carried out by Afghan nationals or people associated with Afghanistan's security forces.

He said the TTP and other militant groups were carrying out attacks inside Pakistan with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and Pakistan would continue to target the TTP and its support infrastructure.

World.title: Coercion, control and high demands: How cults squash their members’ identities
World.content:
A 15-month parliamentary inquiry has defined what a “high-control” organisation is and proposed that their leaders be subject to criminal charges. How it might work is another question.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Laura McConnell was kicked out of her family and the religious cult they raised her in, she went to Centrelink so she could feed herself, a counsellor to work through her issues, and a doctor for a check-up. None of them understood what she was telling them. Laura McConnell, who was kicked out of the Two-by-Twos cult as a teenager. “They just didn’t have the vocabulary,” McConnell says. She was a teenager, so Centrelink wanted a form signed by a parent or guardian – which was impossible. The GP said, “All the women in your religion are depressed – I don’t know what to do for you.” The counsellor gave McConnell the number of a priest, but her group relied on lay preachers, so she “grew up thinking that, to speak to a priest is to speak to the devil”. “I just shut down and didn’t talk to a counsellor for years because I thought that’s where I’d be sent … I found myself in a world I didn’t know anything about, with no language to describe what had happened to me.” All this happened 27 years ago, but McConnell said she helped people leaving the group today who still struggled with the same problems.



Children’s ‘entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it’. Crossing the line: Coercion and harm in high‑control groups McConnell was born and raised in an ultra-strict Christian sect known as Two-by-Twos – but ignorance about the practices of such “high-control groups” is almost universal. Last week, a Victorian parliamentary committee tried to find a language to combat that ignorance. It defined the features of groups sometimes known as cults, and recommended better training for police and child protection workers. It also recommended the Law Reform Commission formulate a new criminal offence for “group-based coercion” to prosecute the leaders of such groups. Patrick McIvor, a former member of a high-control organisation and a counsellor and policy consultant, said “the development of shared language that we haven’t had before” was the committee’s most significant finding. Patrick McIvor, former member of City Builders church and now a counsellor and policy consultant. “People have talked about this experience of not being able to know or name what they’ve been through, especially kids who have grown up in this environment,” McIvor said. “They have felt they’ve had to try to translate themselves into existing categories or terms that people understand.”



It’s unclear how many people are part of high-control groups, but the committee chair, Labor MP Ella George, said her 15-month inquiry had received more than 600 submissions and responses to questions from Victorians, and “to me that speaks to the size of the issue”. George said she had found the evidence she’d heard “heartbreaking and devastating”. Related Article Victorian Parliament Laws failing to protect cult survivors, inquiry finds Her report says the beliefs of these groups are almost immaterial – they can be “religious, commercial enterprise, therapeutic or wellness communities, or any other type of group structure”. What makes them a problem are their practices. The committee found the coercive control these groups exercise over their members – whether they are born into them or are recruited – suppresses their capacity to act, think or live independently. The groups demand ideological or religious purity, they surveil and monitor their members’ activities and patrol their thoughts. They also foster an “us versus them” mindset towards the broader community. The threat of public humiliation or excommunication fosters fear and keeps people under the thumb. Cumulatively, it means members rely on the group for their identity, self-worth, morality, and decision-making – while questioning and critical thinking are punished.



The committee found these practices caused life-long psychological damage. People live in a state of threat, anxiety and hypervigilance, often even well after they have left the group. The erosion of individual autonomy and self‑trust means people often struggle to form or maintain their identity. Children, such as McConnell, who were born into such groups were even more vulnerable than those who were recruited. “Their entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it,” the committee found. Children schooled at home or by the group are worse off because of severely constrained access to “safe adults” outside the group. Healthy groups, by contrast, were transparent and gave their members choice and the freedom to question or refuse, and the ability to leave the group without fear of punishment, the report found. “People also have the right to be free from religion,” McIvor said. Cassie Davies, who was born into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, said the church’s practices had suppressed her identity, and, as a woman, had “boxed me in” to a framework of what was acceptable and not acceptable. “The suppression of any sort of sexual exploration, the complete taboo of the subject, all of that is completely emotionally abusive of children,” she added.



Cassie Davies, who is happily out of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. Establishing who to blame, though, was complex, Davies said. “Who’s the perpetrator? My mum is – but that’s because she believes that’s right, and that’s how her identity has been formed.” Davies did not give evidence to the Victorian parliamentary inquiry. A Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman said the church had not been approached by the committee, and “its report and findings have nothing at all to do with our church”. Asked about coercive practices, the spokesman said “none of this describes life in our church. This report is not about us.” Among the committee’s recommendations are that the charities regulator, ACNC, abolish the category of “basic religious charity”, under which a number of high-control organisations are exempt from key governance and reporting obligations. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations God, Christ, man, woman: The ‘divine order’ that defines life for Exclusive Brethren women The committee said its proposed new criminal offence would be similar to coercive control offences for family violence that have been introduced in some jurisdictions and promised in Victoria, but different in crucial ways. It said criminal culpability should focus on leaders – “those who create, maintain and benefit from systems of control”. The “apparent consent or compliance” of a victim should not be a defence if it was produced by coercion.

World.title: ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet
World.content:
CultureMusicalsStage shows ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet Kerrie O'Brien August 3, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite having won some of Britain and America’s highest theatre awards, and performing opposite Helen Mirren and Dustin Hoffman, Nathaniel Parker has never sung on stage. That’s all about to change: the English actor best-known to Australian audiences for his roles in the BBC’s The Inspector Lynley Mysteries and Merlin is set to make his musical theatre debut in My Fair Lady in Sydney next month. Nathaniel Parker will star as Professor Henry Higgins alongside Australian soprano Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady, which opens in September. Simon Schluter “I’m like a kid in a comedy store. This is a whole new game,” he says. “This is like, I don’t know, it’s like a promotion towards the end of my career.” Playing Eliza Dolittle is Melbourne-based Claire Lyon, no stranger to musical theatre. Best known for playing Christine in The Phantom of the Opera, the soprano says it’s the role of a lifetime. She spends 85 per cent of the show on stage and must master not only a Cockney accent but that of a plummy English toff as well. Luckily, her mum and grandparents are from north London, so something of the accent is in her DNA.



My Fair Lady tells the story of a flower seller on the streets of London being “discovered” by professor of phonetics Henry Higgins, who makes a bet with a friend that he can transform her from a poor commoner into a duchess. Julie Andrews and Rex Harrison in the original stage production of ‘My Fair Lady’. Over the years, the show has been criticised for being misogynistic; back home in England when Parker talked about playing Higgins, several people described the character as exactly that. But the 64-year-old disagrees. “I think that’s the wrong word,” he says. “He’s sexist, unbelievably sexist. The most sexist man I’ve ever played – and I played Henry VIII for two years [in the stage adaptations of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall books]. But he doesn’t hate women. He doesn’t hate his mother, he doesn’t hate Mrs Pearce. He just doesn’t understand the first thing about them, so he’s kept them at a distance.” That said, Parker admits he is “still figuring out the way to say those awfully sexist lines” that come up. “I can feel myself being punched by various friends of mine,” he says. “I think the reason he gets that extreme is because he doesn’t understand the turmoil inside that this woman has caused.”



Lyon argues that the musical, which is based on George Bernard Shaw’s play Pygmalion, written in 1913 at the height of the Suffragette movement, was created and is set in a very different era and should be honoured as an historical work of art, not altered to suit contemporary norms. When she and Parker spoke with Dame Julie Andrews (who at 20 played Eliza in the original Broadway version) via Zoom last week, they discussed its origins. “Things have been tweaked for sure, but I think of Eliza as an incredibly strong young woman. She’s a fighter. She speaks her mind,” Lyon says. “She stands up to a man who is in a different class to her, who’s her senior, and she holds her own. She fights back, and wins him over in the end.” Australian stage royalty Reg Livermore and Robyn Nevin also appear in the much-loved musical, as Alfred P. Doolittle and Mrs Higgins respectively, with Tony Llewellyn-Jones as Colonel Hugh Pickering. Anne Wood plays Mrs Pearce, David Whitney is Karpathy, and Freddy Hellier makes his main stage musical theatre debut as Freddy Eynsford-Hill.



For Parker and Lyon, My Fair Lady is one of the best musicals ever written. It nails all the key components; the writing, the songs and the choreography, not to mention the costumes, are glorious, says Lyon. It’s a feast for the ears, a feast for the eyes and great for the soul, she adds. Classic numbers include Wouldn’t It Be Loverly, The Rain in Spain, I Could Have Danced All Night and Higgins’ infamous Why Can’t a Woman Be More Like a Man? Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle. When the Lerner and Loewe production premiered on Broadway in 1956 starring Andrews as Eliza and Rex Harrison as Higgins, it was an instant hit, winning six Tony Awards. Audrey Hepburn starred in the lead role in the 1964 film version, with Harrison again as the professor; ghost singer Marni Nixon sang Hepburn’s songs. Now celebrating its 70th anniversary, the show is directed by Karen Johnson Mortimer; it is presented by Opera Australia and John Frost.



Parker quips that none of his songs are well-known because Harrison spoke rather than sang them in his portrayals. The British veteran of stage and screen no doubt hopes that will change when Australian audiences see him make his musical debut, the first time in decades he’s sung outside his dressing room. My Fair Lady is at the Sydney Opera House from September and Arts Centre Melbourne from November. Details: opera.org.au

World.title: ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street Stan Choe August 3, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose to finish a wild July for Wall Street as Amazon leaped, Apple sank and rising oil prices worsened worries about inflation staying high. The S&P 500 climbed 0.7 per cent after veering between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones added 276 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1 per cent after briefly losing all of an early 1.3 per cent jump. Wall Street closed a losing month with gains on Friday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to start the week lower, with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 85 points, or 1 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.55¢. August reporting season kicks into gear this week, with News Corp and AMP among those due up. It’s a fitting finish to July for the US stock market, which lurched up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and worries grew about whether Big Tech’s massive investments in artificial-intelligence technology will translate into profits and whether chipmaker stocks soared too high in the euphoria around AI.



Friday’s gains sent the S&P 500 to its first winning week in three, but the main measure of the US stock market nevertheless finished the month with a tiny loss. Amazon led the market with a leap of 15.3 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its profit more than tripled from a year earlier, thanks in part to an acceleration of growth in its cloud computing business. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Healthscope meets landlords to head off private equity break-up threat Analysts said that could be a signal Amazon’s huge AI investments are paying off, and Amazon increased its forecast for how much it will spend on investments this year. The reaction was similar to what Microsoft got a day before, when its stock soared to its best day in nearly 18 years on signals that its AI investments may also be yielding higher profits.



Chip companies selling the processors and computer memory that such “hyperscalers” are scrambling to buy swung sharply again on Friday. Micron Technology, for example, went from an early jump of 6.4 per cent to a loss of 6.5 per cent before finishing with a fall of 5.9 per cent. More firmly on the losing end of Wall Street was Apple, which dropped 7.4 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than expected. Its forecast for revenue growth in the current quarter fell short of expectations, which executives pinned on a supply crunch in components getting vacuumed up in the AI boom. All told, the S&P 500 rose 52.09 points to 7,489.72. The Dow Jones added 276.97 to 52,485.03, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 251.68 to 25,373.85. The gains came despite another rise in oil prices as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.2 per cent to settle at $US87.93 after careening between $US72 and $US102 earlier in July.



Higher oil prices have pushed the cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.11 across the United States, up from $US3.85 a month ago, according to AAA. More expensive oil also puts upward pressure on prices for virtually every product that rides on a ship, plane or truck before getting to a customer. The worries about inflation sent yields in the bond market even higher. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.71 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Thursday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran sent oil prices shooting higher. That’s a notable move for the yield, which moves higher when investors’ expectations for inflation, economic growth and other factors in upcoming years are rising. The leap for the 10-year yield has already sent the average long-term US mortgage rate to its highest level in a year. Longer-term yields jumped on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve’s chairman, Kevin Warsh, promised again to get inflation back down to 2 per cent but refused to say how he plans to get it there. The Fed voted again to keep its main interest rate steady on Wednesday, even though inflation remains well above 2 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Whistleblowers The dismantling of KPMG is about to begin Colin Kruger Senior business reporter Hikes to rates by the Fed could restrain inflation, but they could also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates instead of higher. Warsh has told financial markets that he does not want to give hints about what the Fed will do with interest rates, saying he wants to get direct, “unfiltered” messages from them rather than echoes back of what the Fed has suggested. But “without clarifying why action was or wasn’t taken already, it’s hard to see how statements about being committed to hitting its inflation target aren’t just a bluff,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. “The Fed is facing a growing credibility problem,” economists at Bank of America wrote in a report. Unless data comes in showing less pressure on inflation in the interim, “it is imperative for the Fed to pass the September test by hiking rates and delivering an internally consistent narrative.”



In stock markets abroad, the swings were even wilder for chip stocks. Seoul’s Kospi index soared 17.9 per cent for its best day in history. The index is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and both surged at least 26.8 per cent on Friday. The Kospi, though, still lost 22 per cent in July despite Friday’s historic move. That’s after it more than doubled in the first six months of the year.
